briefing.text: Size-factor target for 'global scale log normalization' changes the final value. scanpy's sc.pp.normalize_total defaults to target_sum=None, which rescales each cell to the MEDIAN library size. 'Global-scaling normalization' is the Seurat LogNormalize wording: divide each cell by its total counts, multiply by a fixed scale factor of 10,000, then natural log1p. Because log1p is non-linear, the later z-score is NOT invariant to the scale factor (1e4 vs median vs 1e6) or to the pseudocount, so the two readings give different answers. The library's reading (from the scanpy and Seurat documentation, not from anything about how this task is graded) is to pass the target explicitly: sc.pp.normalize_total(adata, target_sum=1e4), then sc.pp.log1p(adata), then scale, in that order, with exclude_highly_expressed left False. Do not rely on the default. An explicit target also avoids a version quirk: with target_sum=None, scanpy 1.11.2-1.12.3 computes the median over non-zero-count cells for dense arrays but the plain median for CSR matrices (fixed in 1.12.4), so a median-based result can change if X is converted to sparse. The log base (ln/log2/log10 of 1+x) does not matter: it is a constant factor that cancels in the z-score, so spend no effort on it. Check: compute the final value under target_sum=1e4 and under target_sum=None, record how far apart they are, and state which one you report and why.
briefing.reason: The default scanpy call and the fixed 1e4 scale factor give different final z-scores for the same cell; the team must choose deliberately rather than inherit a default.

briefing.text: Z-score clipping can silently replace the reported value. sc.pp.scale defaults to max_value=None (no clipping), but the legacy scanpy tutorial calls sc.pp.scale(adata, max_value=10) and Seurat ScaleData clips at scale.max=10 by default. The cell with the highest raw count of a marker gene is exactly the kind of outlier whose z-score can exceed 10; a clipped pipeline then returns exactly 10.0 instead of the true z. Check: compute the unclipped z for the target cell and gene and see whether |z| > 10; a result of exactly 10.0 is the signature of clipping. The task text says only 'z-score scale' and names no clip, so the library's literal reading is plain sc.pp.scale(adata) with defaults (no max_value). If the unclipped value exceeds 10, the two conventions disagree: report the unclipped value and record the clipped alternative in your notes.
briefing.reason: Copying max_value=10 from a tutorial template could change the answer for precisely the outlier cell this task targets.

briefing.text: Select the cell on the untouched raw integer matrix, before any normalization, and make sure that matrix really is still raw. (1) After depth normalization the cell with the highest normalized or scaled value is often a different, shallower cell, so an argmax taken after normalize_total/log1p/scale picks the wrong cell. Take the argmax first and store the obs_name, then index the final matrix by that stored name. (2) Ties: raw counts are small integers, several cells can share the maximum, and tied cells have different library sizes and so different final values. Count them with (col == col.max()).sum(). If tied, np.argmax's first occurrence is the conventional pick, but report the tie and the final values of all tied cells in your notes. (3) scanpy works in place: normalize_total, log1p and scale overwrite adata.X, and a 'saved' reference made without .copy() (counts = adata.X, adata.layers['counts'] = adata.X, adata.raw = adata) can alias the same array and be normalized too, so a later 'raw argmax' is computed on normalized values. The library reports this file has no layers and no .raw and that X is a dense int64 array; verify that on load. Before normalizing, assert X is non-negative integers and extract the gene's raw column with .copy(); after normalizing, assert the saved column is still integer-valued. Never normalize twice (scanpy warns 'adata.X seems to be already log-transformed'); if in doubt, reload the file.
briefing.reason: Picking the cell after normalization, on an aliased array, or ignoring a tie yields the value of a different cell, which is a wrong answer however correct the normalization is.

briefing.text: Do not add filtering or subsetting steps: the z-score depends on which cells and genes are in the matrix. Each gene's mean and sd are taken over the cells present at scaling time, and each cell's size factor is its total over the genes present at normalization time. Any filter_cells/filter_genes, QC removal, highly-variable-gene subsetting or regress_out carried over from a 'standard pipeline' template changes the final value, and HVG subsetting can drop the gene of interest altogether (Seurat ScaleData scales only variable features by default). The task says only to normalize and scale 'the given .h5ad', so apply normalize_total -> log1p -> scale to all cells and all genes. The library reports the matrix as 6420 cells x 19918 genes and that obs already carries n_genes, suggesting cell filtering was done upstream. Check: confirm adata.shape is identical from load to the final value and that the gene is still in var_names after scaling.
briefing.reason: Template preprocessing steps are easy to include by habit and each one shifts the gene's mean/sd or the cell's size factor, changing the reported number.

briefing.text: Confirm the gene lookup is unambiguous before using it. Gene symbols are case-sensitive (mouse 'Mrc1' vs human 'MRC1'), var_names can be non-unique (duplicates make adata[:, 'Mrc1'] ambiguous, and var_names_make_unique renames later copies to 'Mrc1-1'), and some files index by Ensembl ID with symbols in a var column. The library reports that var in this file has only an index and no extra columns. Check: (adata.var_names == 'Mrc1').sum() must equal 1, adata.var_names.is_unique should be True, and adata.var_names.get_loc('Mrc1') should return a single integer. If the symbol is duplicated, do not sum or pick one silently; report it. If it is absent, look for a case variant before concluding anything.
briefing.reason: A one-line check that guards against reading the wrong or a duplicated gene column, which would change both the selected cell and the value.

Each computed the alternative, saw that the two differ in the first decimal place, and chose by convention; no check on the task wording or the data was used to decide.

Team B recorded no pitfalls_checked at all and did not record the tie, aliasing or hand-recomputation checks in the form the library asked for; its checks_run list covers ties and duplicates but not an independent recomputation.
second_readings: 'Global scale' could mean a fixed global constant (10,000, or one million) or a single data-derived global target such as the median or mean library size (the default of the common Python tool). The task names no number.

'The final normalized value' could mean the z-scored value (after both steps) or the log-normalized value before z-scoring; 'final' favours the first but the word 'normalized' is used in the task for the log-normalization step.
'z-score scale' could be run with or without the clip at 10 that some standard pipelines apply; both teams showed the clip has no effect here, so this reading is closed.
challenge.verdict: Moderate trust. The mechanics (which cell, order of steps, no clipping effect, no ties) are simple and were checked by both teams, but the one choice that moves the answer in the first decimal place, the scale-factor target, was settled by both teams from the same library note rather than independently, and Team B's own plan had been the other reading, so the agreement adds little on that point.

findings.question: How is 'global scale' / 'global-scaling' log normalization defined in Seurat, scanpy, Bioconductor and tools built on them: a fixed factor (1e4 or 1e6) or also a data-derived target such as the median library size?
findings.answer: 'Global-scaling' is Seurat's term, and it means a fixed factor of 10,000. Seurat pbmc3k tutorial: 'By default, we employ a global-scaling normalization method "LogNormalize" that normalizes the feature expression measurements for each cell by the total expression, multiplies this by a scale factor (10,000 by default), and log-transforms the result.' NormalizeData reference: 'LogNormalize: Feature counts for each cell are divided by the total counts for that cell and multiplied by the scale.factor. This is then natural-log transformed using log1p', with scale.factor = 10000 by default. 1e6 (CPM) appears only under method 'RC' (relative counts, no log). None of the scanpy pages I read uses the phrase 'global scaling'. Scanpy's normalize_total with target_sum=None (the default) normalizes each cell so that 'each observation (cell) has a total count equal to the median of total counts for observations (cells) before normalization', and the current tutorial calls this 'median count depth normalization'. Bioconductor OSCA uses 'scaling normalization' / 'library size normalization', with size factors scaled so that 'the mean size factor across all cells is equal to 1' (a data-derived target), and does not call it 'global'. In the sources read, the phrase goes with dividing by each cell's total and multiplying by a fixed 1e4. None of them uses it for a median target. Caveat: I did not check every workflow or assistant tool, so I cannot rule out looser use elsewhere.

findings.question: Which size-factor target do the current official scanpy tutorials and the legacy scanpy clustering tutorial each use in sc.pp.normalize_total, which z-score clip (if any) does each pass to sc.pp.scale, and has the recommended call changed?
findings.answer: Yes, it changed. Legacy pbmc3k tutorial: sc.pp.normalize_total(adata, target_sum=1e4) ('Total-count normalize (library-size correct) the data matrix X to 10,000 reads per cell'), then sc.pp.log1p, then regress_out and scale. I could not read its exact scale call because the fetched page was cut off before that cell. An earlier library memory note, and several derived workflows seen in search results (pyucell, scmer), give sc.pp.scale(adata, max_value=10). Current scanpy/scverse 'Preprocessing and clustering' tutorial: sc.pp.normalize_total(adata) with the default median target ('# Normalizing to median total counts'; 'We are applying median count depth normalization with log1p transformation'), with no sc.pp.scale step at all (it goes from HVG selection to PCA). sc.pp.scale defaults to max_value=None, which means no clipping. So 'standard' meant 1e4 with clip 10 in the legacy tutorial. The current tutorial uses a median target and does not scale.
findings.confidence: high for the normalize_total targets; medium for the legacy max_value=10 (not seen in a page read this session)
